title: First keep yourself in peace (II.3)
hookLine: a peaceable person does more good than a learned one
tomorrow: what two small things lift a person off the ground?

lines: MORE GOOD THAN A LEARNED ONE.
cards: The group project call is going sideways. Two people are talking over each other. The smartest one on the call has the best argument and is winning it, loudly, and everything gets worse.
Then someone who hasn't said much unmutes. Slow, steady: okay, can we back up a second? The whole call exhales.

The Imitation would bet on that voice. A peaceable person, chapter three of book two says, does more good than a very learned one. But before it lets anyone fix the room, it gives an order of operations.

teach.b: First, the order. Keep yourself in peace first, the chapter says, and then you'll be able to bring peace to others. The Latin calls that person homo pacificus, the peaceable one.
Second, two people side by side.

The peaceable person turns everything toward good. The heated, troubled person turns even good into evil, believes evil easily, suspects everyone, and is neither quiet himself nor lets anyone else be. Third, the mirror.

The heated person keeps careful track of what others owe and forgets what he owes himself. So the Imitation says: be zealous about yourself first, and then you can fairly be zealous about your neighbor.
We're quick to excuse our own deeds, it notes, and slow to accept anyone else's excuse.
Fairer to accuse yourself and excuse your brother. An uncomfortable trade, and a fair one: the same patience you'd ask for, handed out first. Here's one to tell a friend tonight.
The chapter says getting along with good, gentle people is no great thing; everyone likes that.
Living at peace with hard, difficult people is a great grace.

teach.h: A PEACEABLE PERSON DOES MORE GOOD.
teach.b: So the peace it means isn't a calm that needs a calm room. It starts inside, and then it walks into the loud one. That's why the brilliant argument can wait thirty seconds while the arguer breathes.

how: Catholics who read the Imitation often take one chapter slowly, and many bring its counsels into the examination of conscience, asking where they judged others quickly or excused themselves.

games.q: what does “first keep yourself in peace” mean?
o: settle your own heart before bringing peace to others
stay out of conflict so you never lose your calm
calm others down before you deal with yourself

games.q: the peaceable and the heated — tap the pairs.

s: the Imitation says the most learned person does the most good
it says a peaceable person does more good than a very learned one.
the chapter calls peace with difficult people a great grace
living with good, gentle people is no great thing; living peaceably with hard ones is.
keeping yourself in peace means avoiding other people's problems
it's the first step: peace in you, so you can bring peace to others.

games.q: your parents are arguing about money in the kitchen, and you're about to jump in with the obvious fix. by chapter three of book two, what comes first?
o: settle yourself first, then speak if it helps.
jump in now with the fix before it gets worse.
leave the house so you stay out of their trouble.
games.why: keep yourself in peace first, the chapter says, and then you can bring peace to others. the fix can wait a breath.

practice: Sit up and let your shoulders drop, your jaw loosen, your hands rest open on your knees. Bring to mind one person who will need something from you soon, and stay in that posture until you can picture them without bracing. No rush.
If you pray, ask for peace in you first, and then in them.

wordCard.voice: First keep yourself in peace. The Imitation's order: settle your own heart, and then you can bring peace to someone else.

orig.note: Latin, from the Imitation II.3: the peaceable person, who does more good than a very learned one.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: peace first, even when the loudest argument in the room happens to be yours. Talk tomorrow.

sources.ref: The Imitation of Christ II.3 (homo pacificus)
sources.tr: public domain (original): the Latin of the Imitation
